(CNN) -- Three former guerrilla leaders -- who helped command what one activist called "one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days" -- were sentenced Wednesday in Freetown, Sierra Leone, for crimes against humanity. Amputee victims of Sierra Leone's civil war take part in football training at a beach in Freetown. The U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone found the men guilty in February of crimes that included murder, rape, sexual slavery and forced marriages stemming from a civil war that lasted from March 1991 to January 2002. They were arrested in March 2003, said Peter Anderson, spokesman for the U.N. court. The rebels -- former leaders in the Revolutionary United Front guerrilla movement -- were known for hacking off civilians' hands and feet during the war, which stood out for its viciousness even on a a continent that has suffered many horrific conflicts. Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet of Canada read the sentences. Former Revolutionary United Front "interim leader" Issa Hassan Sesay was sentenced to 52 years in prison, former commander Morris Kallon to 40 years, and former chief of security Augustine Gbao to 25 years. Sesay and Kallon had been found guilty on 16 counts, and Gbao was found guilty on 14. The former rebels received credit for the six years each already has served in prison, Anderson told CNN. He said they will be imprisoned in another country, maybe Rwanda, because the prisons in Sierra Leone do not meet the standards of the U.N. court. Kallon was the only one of the three to express sorrow at his sentencing, Anderson said. "He really had made a genuine expression of remorse," which is considered a stronger statement than regret, the court spokesman added. The court noted several mitigating factors at the sentencing, but "in view of the gravity of the crimes, their impact was limited," a statement from the court said. The court noted that the crimes "were committed upon a massive scale across several districts of Sierra Leone" and that "the impact of all these crimes upon the Sierra Leonean society has been enormous." "The Chamber concluded that the inherent gravity of the criminal acts for which Sesay, Kallon and Gbao have been convicted is exceptionally high," the statement said. Corinne Dufka, a senior researcher in Human Rights Watch's Africa division, had called the verdict "very significant." "The RUF were renowned for leading one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days. Everyone knows about the signature atrocity of limb amputation, but there was also horrific sexual violence, abductions, use of child soldiers and forced marriages," she told CNN by phone from Senegal in West Africa. Eight people have been convicted of war crimes connected with the conflict -- some on the rebels' side and some on the government's. The U.N. Special Court's mandate is to try only "those who bear greatest responsibility for atrocities committed in Sierra Leone." The trial of Sesay, Kallon and Gbao lasted nearly five years. The three had pleaded not guilty on all counts. The Special Court cannot impose the death penalty. The Revolutionary United Front seized most of Sierra Leone from the government and fought international and African peacekeepers. International forces retook the capital, Freetown, in 2000. The trial of the three former leaders was the last of three to be held at the Special Court. Former Liberian President Charles Taylor is on trial separately at an international court in The Hague, Netherlands, for his role in the conflict. The prosecution rested in the Taylor case in January after a year of presenting its arguments. Sierra Leone is known for its diamond wealth, but 70 percent of the population lives below the poverty line. The Special Court is an independent tribunal established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leone government. It is mandated to bring to justice those most responsible for atrocities committed in Sierra Leone after November 30, 1996.

(CNN) — A court in Freetown, Sierra Leone, handed prison terms Wednesday to three former guerrilla commanders who helped lead what a human rights advocate described as among the most savage rebel organizations of modern times.

In February, the U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted the men of crimes against humanity arising from the country’s civil war, which ran from March 1991 until January 2002. The offenses included killing, rape, sexual enslavement and forced marriage.

Peter Anderson, a spokesman for the U.N.-backed tribunal, said the three were arrested in March 2003. All had been senior figures in the Revolutionary United Front, or RUF, whose fighters became notorious for cutting off civilians’ hands and feet. The conflict was considered exceptionally cruel even by the standards of a continent that has experienced numerous devastating wars.

Canadian Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet announced the punishments. Issa Hassan Sesay, a former RUF “interim leader,” received a 52-year sentence. Former commander Morris Kallon was given 40 years, while Augustine Gbao, the group’s former security chief, was sentenced to 25 years.

Sesay and Kallon were each convicted on 16 charges, while Gbao was found guilty on 14. Anderson told CNN that all three would receive credit for the six years they had already spent behind bars.

Because Sierra Leone’s prisons do not satisfy the U.N. court’s requirements, the men will serve their terms in another country, Anderson said. Rwanda was mentioned as a possible location.

According to Anderson, Kallon was the only defendant to voice sorrow during sentencing. The spokesman said Kallon had shown “a genuine expression of remorse,” which the court regarded as more meaningful than simply expressing regret.

Although the judges considered several circumstances that could lessen the sentences, the court said those factors carried little weight because of the seriousness of the offenses. In a statement, it emphasized that the crimes occurred on a vast scale in multiple districts and had an enormous effect on Sierra Leonean society.

The chamber determined that the underlying seriousness of the acts for which Sesay, Kallon and Gbao were convicted was extraordinarily high, the statement added.

Corinne Dufka, a senior researcher with Human Rights Watch’s Africa division, previously described the verdict as highly important. Speaking to CNN by telephone from Senegal, she said the RUF was widely known as one of the modern era’s most brutal insurgent groups. While its defining atrocity was the amputation of limbs, she noted that its members also committed appalling sexual violence, abducted people, recruited child soldiers and imposed forced marriages.

Eight individuals have been convicted of war crimes related to the Sierra Leone conflict, including people aligned with both the rebels and the government. The Special Court’s authority extends only to prosecuting those considered most responsible for the atrocities.

The proceedings against Sesay, Kallon and Gbao continued for almost five years. Each man denied every charge. The tribunal does not have the power to impose capital punishment.

During the war, the RUF captured most of Sierra Leone from government control and battled both African and international peacekeeping forces. International troops regained Freetown, the capital, in 2000.

The case against the three former commanders was the third and final trial conducted at the Special Court. Former Liberian President Charles Taylor is being tried separately before an international tribunal in The Hague, Netherlands, over his alleged involvement in the Sierra Leone conflict. Prosecutors concluded their case against Taylor in January after spending a year presenting evidence and arguments.

Sierra Leone possesses substantial diamond resources, yet 70 percent of its people live below the poverty threshold. Amputees injured during the civil war have taken part in soccer training on a Freetown beach.

Created jointly by the United Nations and Sierra Leone’s government, the Special Court is an independent judicial body. Its mandate is to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for atrocities carried out in Sierra Leone after November 30, 1996.

counterfactuals.output:
# Former Sierra Leone rebel leaders sentenced for war crimes

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone —** Three former leaders of Sierra Leone’s Revolutionary United Front were handed lengthy prison terms Wednesday for crimes committed during the country’s brutal civil war.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone sentenced former RUF interim leader Issa Sesay to 52 years in prison, senior commander Morris Kallon to 40 years and commander Augustine Gbao to 25 years.

The men were convicted in February 2009 of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, mutilation and the recruitment of child soldiers. Sesay and Kallon were also convicted in connection with attacks on United Nations peacekeepers.

Prosecutors said the RUF waged a campaign of terror against civilians during Sierra Leone’s 1991-2002 conflict. The rebel group became notorious for amputating victims’ limbs, abducting women and children, and forcing captives to fight or work for its forces.

The trial marked the first time an international tribunal convicted defendants of forced marriage as a crime against humanity.

Judges said the sentences reflected the gravity and widespread nature of the crimes. Although the court’s statute allows life imprisonment, the prosecution had requested fixed terms.

Sierra Leone’s civil war left tens of thousands of people dead and displaced more than 2 million. The conflict was fueled in part by the illicit diamond trade, with rebels using diamonds to finance weapons and military operations.

The three men will receive credit for time already spent in detention. Because the Special Court does not have a long-term prison facility, they are expected to serve their sentences outside Sierra Leone under arrangements with other countries.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the prison sentences handed down by the U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone to Issa Hassan Sesay, Morris Kallon, and Augustine Gbao, including their convictions, mitigating factors, and the broader history of the conflict.
counterfactuals.output:
## Sentences imposed

On 8 April 2009, the U.N.-backed Special Court for Sierra Leone sentenced three senior leaders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF):

| Defendant | RUF role | Sentence |
|---|---|---:|
| **Issa Hassan Sesay** | Senior commander and, after Foday Sankoh’s arrest, effective head of the RUF | **52 years’ imprisonment** |
| **Morris Kallon** | Senior RUF commander | **40 years’ imprisonment** |
| **Augustine Gbao** | Senior commander and influential RUF official | **25 years’ imprisonment** |

The terms on the individual counts were ordered to run concurrently, with credit for time already spent in detention. The Appeals Chamber later left the overall sentences in place. The men were subsequently transferred to Rwanda to serve their terms because Sierra Leone lacked an appropriate long-term facility.

## Convictions

In February 2009, the Trial Chamber found Sesay and Kallon guilty on **16 of 18 counts** and Gbao on **14 of 18 counts**. The convictions covered crimes against humanity, war crimes, and other serious violations of international humanitarian law committed primarily between 1996 and 2000.

They included responsibility for:

- Murder and extermination  
- Terrorizing and collectively punishing civilians  
- Mutilation, beatings, and other cruel or inhumane treatment  
- Rape, sexual slavery, and forced marriage  
- Enslavement and forced labor  
- Pillage and the burning or destruction of civilian property  
- Conscripting or using children under 15 in armed conflict  
- Attacks on U.N. peacekeepers and associated personnel  

The case was especially significant because it was among the first international judgments to treat **forced marriage as a distinct crime against humanity** and to impose convictions for attacks against U.N. peacekeepers.

The chamber found that the atrocities were not isolated excesses. They formed part of organized RUF operations and a campaign designed to control territory, obtain labor and resources, punish suspected opponents, and spread terror. Sesay received the longest sentence because of his senior authority, extensive participation, and responsibility for a particularly broad range of crimes.

## Mitigating considerations

The judges considered each defendant’s personal circumstances, conduct, and role in the peace process, but held that mitigation carried limited weight beside the scale and brutality of the offenses.

- **Sesay:** The chamber gave meaningful credit to his later contribution to the peace process, including steps that assisted disarmament and helped bring the war to an end. Nonetheless, it concluded that this could not outweigh his leadership role and responsibility for widespread atrocities.
- **Kallon:** The judges considered his expressions of remorse, his personal and family circumstances, his conduct in detention, and evidence concerning his involvement in later peace and disarmament efforts. These factors reduced but did not substantially diminish the sentence required by the crimes.
- **Gbao:** His age, background, personal circumstances, and evidence of positive conduct or character were considered. His lower position relative to Sesay and the narrower range of convictions also contributed to a shorter sentence, although 25 years was still deemed necessary.

The court stressed that ordinary family hardship, lack of education, good behavior while detained, and similar factors deserved only modest weight in prosecutions involving mass atrocities.

## Historical context

Sierra Leone’s civil war began in **March 1991**, when the RUF, led by **Foday Sankoh** and supported from neighboring Liberia, entered eastern Sierra Leone. The movement claimed to oppose corruption and exclusion, but its forces became notorious for attacks on civilians, including amputations, rape, abduction, forced labor, child recruitment, and the looting of diamond-producing areas.

Major developments included:

- **1991–1996:** The RUF expanded through eastern and southern Sierra Leone amid repeated military and political upheaval.
- **1996:** Ahmad Tejan Kabbah was elected president, and an initial peace agreement failed.
- **1997:** The Armed Forces Revolutionary Council overthrew Kabbah and invited the RUF into a joint junta.
- **1998:** West African forces restored Kabbah, but the RUF and its allies continued the war.
- **January 1999:** Rebel forces attacked Freetown in an exceptionally brutal offensive marked by mass killings, amputations, rape, abduction, and destruction.
- **July 1999:** The Lomé Peace Agreement offered the rebels political participation and a broad domestic amnesty, but violence continued.
- **2000:** RUF forces attacked and detained U.N. peacekeepers. British intervention, regional pressure, and renewed disarmament helped reverse the rebels’ position.
- **January 2002:** The government formally declared the war over.

The conflict killed tens of thousands of people, displaced a large portion of the population, and left many survivors with permanent physical and psychological injuries.

The Special Court was created through a **2002 agreement between the United Nations and Sierra Leone** to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for crimes committed after 30 November 1996. It was a hybrid tribunal combining international and Sierra Leonean law and personnel. Unlike Sierra Leone’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, it imposed criminal penalties; unlike the Lomé amnesty, its jurisdiction allowed prosecution for international crimes. The RUF judgment was one of its central cases and established an extensive judicial record of the movement’s campaign against Sierra Leone’s civilian population.

# Sierra Leone Rebel Leaders Sentenced to Up to 52 Years for Wartime Atrocities

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone — April 8, 2009**

A United Nations-backed court on Wednesday sentenced three former leaders of Sierra Leone’s Revolutionary United Front to prison terms of 52, 40 and 25 years for directing and supporting a campaign of murder, mutilation, rape, forced marriage, child recruitment and other atrocities during the country’s civil war.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone sentenced **Issa Hassan Sesay**, the RUF’s former interim leader, to **52 years** in prison. Senior commander **Morris Kallon** received **40 years**, while the movement’s former “ideological trainer,” **Augustine Gbao**, was sentenced to **25 years**.

The punishment followed their February convictions on multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Sesay and Kallon were found guilty on 16 of 18 counts, while Gbao was convicted on 14 counts.

Judges said the crimes were part of a widespread and systematic assault on Sierra Leone’s civilian population during the 1991-2002 conflict, one of West Africa’s most brutal wars. Tens of thousands of people were killed, and many more were driven from their homes.

## Campaign of terror against civilians

The RUF became notorious for using terror to gain control of territory and diamond-producing regions. Its fighters burned villages, executed civilians and deliberately cut off victims’ hands, arms, ears or other body parts. The amputations were intended to punish communities and spread fear.

The three commanders were held responsible for offenses including:

- Murder and extermination  
- Mutilation and other acts of physical violence  
- Rape and sexual slavery  
- Forced marriage  
- Enslavement and forced labor  
- Recruitment and use of children under 15 as soldiers  
- Pillage and destruction of civilian property  
- Attacks on United Nations peacekeepers  
- Collective punishment and acts intended to terrorize civilians  

Women and girls captured by the rebels were frequently assigned to fighters as so-called “bush wives.” They were forced to perform domestic labor and subjected to repeated sexual violence. The court treated forced marriage as a distinct crime against humanity, making the judgment an important development in international criminal law.

Children abducted by the RUF were trained to fight, carry supplies and guard commanders. Some were forced to commit killings or other atrocities, often after being beaten, threatened or given drugs.

## Why the sentences differed

Sesay received the longest sentence because of his senior position and extensive authority within the rebel organization. He rose through the RUF’s command structure and became its interim leader after founder Foday Sankoh was detained in 2000. Judges found that Sesay exercised substantial operational control over fighters and bore responsibility for crimes committed during major rebel campaigns.

Kallon, another powerful field commander, was sentenced to 40 years for his role in planning, ordering or facilitating operations in which civilians were attacked. The court found that he held significant authority over troops and contributed directly to the RUF’s violent strategy.

Gbao’s 25-year term reflected his lower degree of responsibility compared with Sesay and Kallon, although the judges still considered him a senior figure who exercised influence and authority within the movement.

The chamber imposed separate terms for individual offenses but ordered the sentences to run concurrently, producing the final totals announced Wednesday. The men are to receive credit for the time they have spent in detention since their arrests in 2003.

## Landmark verdict for Sierra Leone

The case was the court’s principal prosecution of the RUF leadership. Sankoh died in custody in 2003 before he could stand trial, leaving Sesay, Kallon and Gbao as the movement’s highest-ranking members to face judgment.

The trial also produced the first international convictions for attacks on United Nations peacekeepers. In 2000, RUF forces seized and detained hundreds of members of the U.N. mission sent to oversee Sierra Leone’s peace process.

Prosecutors said the sentences recognized the exceptional cruelty of crimes inflicted on civilians over years of fighting. Defense lawyers had argued that the men should receive lesser punishment and said they had ultimately participated in efforts to end the war.

All three defendants have the right to appeal their convictions and sentences.

The Special Court was established jointly by the Sierra Leonean government and the United Nations to prosecute those who bore the greatest responsibility for atrocities committed after November 1996. Unlike the international tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, the court sits in the country where most of the crimes occurred.

Wednesday’s sentencing brings one of the court’s most important cases close to completion and marks a decisive legal reckoning for an organization whose name became synonymous with amputations, child soldiers and terror against civilians.

counterfactuals.output:
The Special Court for Sierra Leone in Freetown convicted the three surviving senior Revolutionary United Front leaders—Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon and Augustine Gbao—of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Sierra Leone’s civil war. The court said the evidence established their guilt “beyond reasonable doubt”; Sesay and Kallon were convicted on 16 of 18 counts, and Gbao on 14. They were later sentenced to 52, 40 and 25 years respectively.

Court spokesman Peter Andersen noted the verdict’s precedential importance: “This is the first conviction for forced marriage as a crime against humanity, and it’s the first conviction by an international court for attacks against UN peacekeepers.”

Human Rights Watch researcher Corinne Dufka welcomed the judgment as justice for civilians terrorized by the RUF: “The RUF rebels were notorious for brutal atrocities throughout Sierra Leone’s 11-year armed conflict. These guilty verdicts provide a measure of justice for their victims.”

# Sierra Leone rebel leaders sentenced for war crimes

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone** — Three senior commanders of Sierra Leone’s Revolutionary United Front were sentenced to lengthy prison terms for their roles in a civil war marked by mass killings, amputations, sexual violence and the forced recruitment of children.

The U.N.-backed Special Court for Sierra Leone sentenced former RUF commander **Issa Sesay to 52 years in prison**, **Morris Kallon to 40 years** and **Augustine Gbao to 25 years**. Their convictions and sentences were later upheld on appeal.

The judges found the men responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Sierra Leone’s 1991-2002 conflict. The charges included murder, mutilation, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, enslavement, pillage and the use of child soldiers. Sesay and Kallon were also held responsible for attacks on United Nations peacekeepers.

## A campaign of terror

The RUF became notorious for terrorizing civilians as it fought to seize territory and control the country’s diamond resources. Fighters hacked off victims’ hands, arms and legs, burned villages, executed civilians and abducted women and girls, many of whom were subjected to rape, forced domestic labor and coerced “marriages.”

Children were kidnapped, drugged and forced to fight or commit atrocities. The conflict, which also involved government forces, pro-government militias and other armed groups, left tens of thousands dead and displaced a large part of Sierra Leone’s population.

Sesay rose to become the RUF’s leading commander after founder Foday Sankoh was detained. Kallon was another senior battlefield commander, while Gbao served as an influential military and ideological figure.

## Court created to pursue senior figures

The Special Court for Sierra Leone was established through an agreement between the Sierra Leonean government and the United Nations. Unlike a conventional international tribunal, it was a hybrid court combining international and Sierra Leonean law and personnel.

Its mandate was to prosecute those who bore **“the greatest responsibility”** for serious violations of international humanitarian law and Sierra Leonean law committed in the country since **November 30, 1996**. The court did not attempt to prosecute every participant in the war; it concentrated on senior leaders from the RUF, the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council and the pro-government Civil Defence Forces.

The proceedings contributed important rulings on the recruitment and use of child soldiers and on forced marriage as a distinct crime against humanity. The court was also the first internationalized tribunal to sit primarily in the country where the crimes occurred, although some proceedings were transferred for security reasons.

## Charles Taylor tried separately

Former Liberian President **Charles Taylor** was prosecuted in a separate case. Prosecutors alleged that Taylor supported the RUF and allied rebels with weapons, ammunition and other assistance in exchange for diamonds, while helping plan or encourage their operations.

Although Taylor was indicted by the Sierra Leone court, his trial was moved to **The Hague, Netherlands**, because of concerns that proceedings in Freetown could destabilize the region. He was tried before the Special Court, not the International Criminal Court.

Taylor was ultimately convicted on 11 counts of aiding and abetting war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, rape, mutilation, sexual slavery and the recruitment of child soldiers. He was sentenced to **50 years in prison**, becoming the first former African head of state convicted by an international tribunal for such crimes.

The cases against Sesay, Kallon, Gbao and Taylor represented the central effort to hold senior political and military figures accountable for atrocities committed during one of West Africa’s most brutal conflicts.
